solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Sleuth nails criminal — that describes very old TV show

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so the jumbled letters go around the next piece
criminal means crooked or bent, so the letters of the two opening words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A detective nails a crook, in a nod to some ancient television programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' scrambles SLEUTHNAILS, and 'describes' wraps those letters round V. The Sullivans was an Australian wartime family drama of the late 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sullivans is an Australian drama series first broadcast in 1976, so a programme from long ago.

clue.text: Glossy magazine featuring one northern troublemaker

indicators.note: a magazine featuring something has it within its pages, so the next piece goes inside

parts.note: Hello! is a British celebrity magazine printed on glossy paper
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A celebrity magazine runs a piece on a single northern rabble-rouser.
explanation.definitionFit: A hellion is a rowdy, mischievous person, a synonym for one who stirs up trouble.

clue.text: Good man drably dressed for American TV show

parts.note: ST, short for saint, is the crossword good man
drably dressed is in grey, which an American spells in gray

explanation.surface: A virtuous fellow dresses dully for an American television programme.
explanation.walkthrough: The American spelling GRAY, not British GREY, is what 'for American' asks for. Stingray was a 1960s Gerry Anderson puppet series about a submarine.
explanation.definitionFit: Stingray is a 1960s British children's puppet series, so an example of a television programme.

clue.text: Part of film studio hosting special TV show

indicators.note: a host has a guest inside, so the lot surrounds the next letter

parts.note: a lot, or backlot, is the open ground of a film studio where sets are built

explanation.surface: Part of a movie studio puts on a one-off programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Lost is an American drama series about plane-crash survivors, an example of a television programme.

clue.text: Failing to have match shortened, icy and slippery outside

indicators.note: the word icy is placed outside, so its letters surround the rest

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: slippery means shifting about, so the letters of the word and are rearranged
shortened means the last letter is cut from the synonym

parts.note: to match something is to equal it

explanation.surface: Someone fails to get a game cut short because the pitch is icy and slippery.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'and' as a mere joiner, but 'slippery' makes it slide into NAD; 'outside' splits the word icy after its first letter to wrap the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A failing is a shortcoming, and inadequacy names that same lack of sufficiency.

clue.text: Where, in Jordan, I'm at my best before noon

definitions.meaning: the place sought is a city in Jordan, its capital

definitions.text: I'm at my best before noon
definitions.meaning: a morning person could call himself an a.m. man, AM being before noon

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits as AM MAN: someone at their best in the morning.
explanation.definitionFit: Amman is the capital city of Jordan; the second sense is a punning morning person.

clue.text: Bird makes air seem fluid

indicators.note: fluid means flowing and changeable, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bird makes the air seem to flow.
explanation.definitionFit: The seriema is a long-legged South American bird of open grassland.

clue.text: Our choice on editing poem's intro — check some lines

indicators.note: editing reworks text, so the letters of the opening two words are rearranged
the intro of a word is its first letter

parts.note: a let is a hindrance or check, as in without let or hindrance

explanation.surface: An editor's choice about the opening of a poem, then a quick check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'editing' rearranges OURCHOICE, 'intro' takes P from poem's, and 'check' is LET in its old sense of obstruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A heroic couplet is a pair of rhyming iambic pentameter lines, so some lines of verse.

clue.text: Loud band, 70s rockers, mostly love this appliance

parts.note: F, forte, is the musical direction for loud
a ridge is a long narrow band or strip of raised ground
Free was a British rock group of the 1970s, known for All Right Now

indicators.note: mostly means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring

explanation.surface: A noisy band, seventies rockers, mostly adore this kitchen appliance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'band' looks like the musical group, but it is a ridge; the group is FREE. 'mostly' cuts ZERO to ZER.
explanation.definitionFit: A fridge-freezer is a kitchen unit combining a refrigerator and a freezer.

clue.text: Where city types hide sticky fingers

parts.note: EC is the postcode area of the City of London, the financial district
a hide is a hiding place, and a lair is the den where an animal hides; the clue's 'Where ... types hide' asks for such places

explanation.surface: Asking where City bankers stash their thieving hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sticky fingers' suggests thieves, but eclairs are finger-shaped iced pastries. City types hiding in the EC district gives EC LAIRS.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclairs are long finger-shaped choux pastries with sticky icing, so a witty description.

clue.text: Engineer married sweetheart

indicators.note: to engineer is to contrive or rearrange, so the letters of married are reworked

explanation.surface: An engineer weds his beloved.
explanation.definitionFit: An admirer is someone who is fond of another, a suitor or beau.

clue.text: Old branch not paid

parts.note: a wing is a branch or section of a building or organisation

explanation.surface: An old offshoot of a firm still hasn't settled its bill.
explanation.definitionFit: Money owing is still due and outstanding, so it has not been settled.

clue.text: TV show character struck down by reporter

indicators.note: a reporter's version is spoken, so the phrase is replaced by one that sounds like it

parts.note: a character is a sign or symbol, and struck down means felled

explanation.surface: A TV personality is attacked, according to a journalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'character' looks like a person in the show, but here it is a written symbol: SIGN FELLED.
explanation.definitionFit: Seinfeld is an American sitcom of the 1990s, an example of a television programme.

clue.text: Mike fills tumbler by one in suitable TV show

indicators.note: to fill something is to sit inside it, so M goes within

parts.note: Jill of the nursery rhyme came tumbling down the hill after Jack
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: the next pieces are placed in the synonym that follows

parts.note: suitable means fit
by as in multiplied by is the times sign X
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Mike pours a drink into a glass beside someone at a fitting television show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tumbler' wants to be a glass; it is Jill, who came tumbling after. Jim'll Fix It was a BBC show of the 1970s and 80s granting viewers' wishes.
explanation.definitionFit: Jim'll Fix It was a long-running BBC programme, so an example of a television show.

clue.text: Juggling act using two balls for catching

indicators.note: juggling tosses things about, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: a ball is round like the letter O, so two of them give OO

explanation.surface: A juggler's act that uses a couple of balls, all about catching them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catching' looks like the juggler's skill but is the definition, in the sense of infectious.
explanation.definitionFit: A catching disease is contagious, passed readily from one person to another.

clue.text: Footballers on vacation manage to produce TV show

parts.note: the FA, the Football Association, governs English football

indicators.note: a word on vacation is emptied, keeping only its outside letters

explanation.surface: Footballers off on holiday manage to put on a television show.
explanation.definitionFit: Fame was a 1980s series set at a New York performing arts school, a television programme.

clue.text: Like 24 as it were, saves one Conservative

indicators.note: as it were flags the playful plural, saves read as two copies of bar

parts.note: save means except, as does bar
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Like the beast in another clue, so to speak, it spares one Tory.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 refers to the answer at 24 across. 'saves' looks like rescue, but it means excepts, and 'as it were' reads the plural as two BARs.
explanation.definitionFit: A brute is savage and cruel, and barbaric describes that same savagery.

clue.text: Turn back on 24

indicators.note: back means the preceding word is read in reverse

parts.note: a turn in a game is a go
re means on or concerning, as in letter headings

explanation.surface: An instruction to switch something back on.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 refers to the answer at 24 across: a monstrous one.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a monstrous, cruel giant, so a fitting match for a brute.

clue.text: Being wild as bank declared responsibility?

indicators.note: declared means said out loud, so the synonym is replaced by a word sounding the same

parts.note: a bank of seats or keys is a row
the buck is responsibility, as in the buck stops here

explanation.surface: Asks whether a bank has openly claimed to be accountable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bank' suggests money, but it is a tier or row.
explanation.definitionFit: A roebuck is a male roe deer, a creature living in the wild.

clue.text: Need to interrupt, casually, less pleasant TV show

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in, so the first synonym goes inside the second

parts.note: badder is a casual, nonstandard form meaning worse or less pleasant
need means lack

explanation.surface: Someone must cut in, offhandedly, on a nastier programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'casually' marks BADDER as slang rather than standard English.
explanation.definitionFit: Blackadder is a BBC historical sitcom, an example of a television programme.

clue.text: One beating dead stranger?

parts.note: rum means odd, so stranger is rummer

explanation.surface: Who killed an unknown person?
explanation.walkthrough: 'stranger' looks like a noun, an outsider, but is the comparative of rum, odd.
explanation.definitionFit: A drummer beats the drums, so one who beats time in a band.

clue.text: Ornament which unfussy fitter possibly holds back

indicators.note: back means the held letters are read in reverse
the words hold the run of letters within them

explanation.surface: Decoration that a no-nonsense fitter might well hold back on.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters YFITTERP sit across 'unfussy fitter possibly' and read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To ornament something is to decorate it, and prettify likewise means to make pretty.

clue.text: TV show coming up is good overall

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means the letters read from bottom to top, in reverse

parts.note: OK means good or acceptable
net means overall, after everything is deducted

explanation.surface: An upcoming programme is fine all round.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenko was a BBC drama about women in a Japanese prison camp, a television programme.

clue.text: One monstrous pinnacle of rock piercing Scottish island

indicators.note: a letter piercing a word is pushed inside it

parts.note: Bute is an island in the Firth of Clyde

indicators.note: the pinnacle of a word is its top, its first letter

explanation.surface: A huge peak of rock pierces an island off Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A brute is a savage, cruel person or beast, one who behaves monstrously.

clue.text: Line that opens my TV show

indicators.note: the letter opens up the exclamation, splitting it apart from within

parts.note: my and gee are both exclamations of surprise

explanation.surface: The opening line of my television programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opens' suggests the start of the show, but L opens up GEE from inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Glee was an American musical comedy-drama series, an example of a television programme.

clue.text: TV show about horses, mostly, and cattle

indicators.note: mostly means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: equine means concerning horses
an ox is one of the cattle

explanation.surface: A programme about horses, for the most part, and cows.
explanation.definitionFit: Equinox was a Channel 4 science documentary series, so an example of a TV programme.

clue.text: US city that is hosting hit TV show

indicators.note: a host holds the guest within, so the next synonym goes inside

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles
ie, id est, means that is
to ram is to hit hard

explanation.surface: An American city puts on a successful television show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US city' looks like the definition, and Laramie is indeed one, but here it gives LA; the show is the 1950s Western series Laramie.
explanation.definitionFit: Laramie was an American Western series of 1959 to 1963, a television programme.

clue.text: Back to back love that man, 20, makes you understand

indicators.note: the back of the following word is its last letter

parts.note: love means nothing, and nowt is northern English for nothing
that man is he
a score is twenty

explanation.surface: Backing a love for that man in a pairing of twenty makes you see things.
explanation.walkthrough: '20' looks like a cross-reference but is simply the number. NOWT is northern English dialect for nothing, like love in tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: To know the score is an idiom for understanding the real situation.
